title: Design exercise: API rate limiter
summary: A classic design exercise: rate limiting for a public API served from twenty gateway nodes, with a 1 ms decision budget and a limiter that must never become the outage. The reference answer keeps token buckets on each node, corrects them from a shared store every 100 ms, fails open by default, and bounds overshoot in numbers. Converted by hand from the module outline's reference answer and its 45-minute script; every number and source is kept.

exercise.prompt: Design the rate limiting for a public HTTP API served from many gateway nodes. Each API key has a limit; callers over the limit get a 429. The product team wants to add tiers and per-endpoint costs later.

constraints.caption: Constraints and numbers.
rows: A per-key limit with a burst; 429 with headers that tell the caller when to retry; policies editable without a deploy.
50,000 requests per second across 20 gateway nodes in one region; 1 million active keys.
Typical limits of 100 requests per second with a burst of 200; a few keys hold 30 to 40 percent of traffic.
derive the per-node rate, the policy data size and the per-node bucket memory yourself
The decision adds under 1 ms at p99; the limiter must never make the API unavailable.
Overshoot of up to 10 percent over a one-second window is acceptable; sustained overshoot is not.
DDoS protection at the network layer, billing.

clarifying_questions.q: Per key, per user or per IP?
clarifying_questions.a: Per key; per IP is a separate abuse limiter.

clarifying_questions.q: What if the shared store is down?
clarifying_questions.a: The API must stay up; limits may loosen, and that must be visible.
Later, via a cost per request.
Per region now; a global view later.

blocks.text: The limiter is a library inside each gateway node plus a shared store, not a separate network hop, because of the latency budget. Local buckets decide; the shared store corrects them a few times per second; a policy service pushes policies that every node caches.

blocks.text: Stripe's write-up describes the token bucket with a centralised bucket host that every request consults; this answer moves the bucket into the node and keeps the shared store as a correction, which trades a little exactness for the round trip. The sliding window counter in the store is the Cloudflare method: two fixed-window counters, the previous one weighted by how much of it overlaps the sliding window.

reference_answer.title: The core flow, step by step

blocks.text: The decision path on one node, and the correction loop behind it.

blocks.title: Decide locally, correct globally
items: Each node holds a token bucket per key sized to its share of the limit: with 20 nodes and random balancing, each node gets about 1/20 of a key's traffic, so each bucket refills at rate/20 with burst/20.
A request takes cost tokens from the key's local bucket; if the bucket is empty the node answers 429 with Retry-After and the RateLimit headers, at no backend cost.
Every 100 ms (assumption) a node reports its counts per active key to the shared store and reads the global count for the last second.

If the global count shows a key over its limit while the local buckets allowed it (uneven balancing, a hot key pinned to few nodes), the node tightens that key's local bucket for the next interval. The shared store therefore corrects, it does not decide; its latency is off the request path.
The store's own cost is 20 nodes times 10 reports per second, each a batch of the node's active keys, which is a few hundred batched writes per second, not 50,000 single ones.

blocks.text: When the shared store is slow or down, the design fails open: nodes keep enforcing local buckets at their share, so each key is still bounded (by at most the number of nodes times its share, in the worst case of all traffic for a key on one node, which balancing makes unlikely). Emit a metric and an alert the moment the store is unreachable.

Fail closed (reject when the store is unreachable) would turn a store outage into an API outage, which breaks the first target; fail closed is the right choice only where the limit protects something that must not be exceeded, such as a payment endpoint with a legal cap, and that is a per-policy flag. This follows the overload guidance of the SRE book's handling-overload chapter (reject cheaply, protect the service, never let the protection become the outage) and the Builders' Library article on load shedding, which measures the service by goodput rather than throughput.

blocks.caption: The hot key: one key at 20,000 requests per second, 40 percent of all traffic.
rows: Pin the key to a dedicated node pair with consistent hashing, so one bucket sees all of it
a hot node; a topology change

blocks.text: Per-endpoint cost is a multiplier on the tokens taken; tiers are just different policies; neither changes the architecture. Azure's throttling pattern describes the same server-side shape: a service that rejects or degrades when a limit is reached, with autoscaling as the slower complement.

blocks.text: The arithmetic is the L3 point: exactness is a product decision with a price, and at ten times the traffic the price of an exact limiter is the budget of a small team.

L1: A token bucket per key and a shared store.
429 with Retry-After and the RateLimit headers, and a clear statement of what happens at the limit.
L2: The local-first design with a correction loop and the latency arithmetic (2,500 decisions per node per second, a few hundred batched store writes per second).
The fail-open argument with its exception (fail closed per policy where a cap is legal or financial).
Hot keys, policy caching, the overshoot bound in numbers, and metrics that show drift.
L3: Whether the product wants a rate limiter, a quota, or both; tiers as policy, not architecture.
The per-tenant fairness framing (the multi-tenancy lesson) and the cost of exactness as a business decision.
How the design behaves during a retry storm from a large customer.

interview_frame.title: A 45-minute interview
items: 0:00 to 0:05: Requirements. Ask: who is limited (API key, user, IP, tenant tier)? What limit shape (requests per second with a burst, or per minute)? What happens on reject (429 with a Retry-After header)? Must limits be exact, or is a small overshoot acceptable? Where does it sit (every edge node, or a central service)? State the numbers you will design for and say them aloud: 50k requests per second at the edge across 20 nodes (chosen for the exercise), 1 million distinct keys, decision latency under 1 ms added at p99, limits of the order of 100 requests per second with a burst of 200. Non-goals: billing, abuse detection, DDoS mitigation.

0:05 to 0:10: API and entities. check(key, cost=1) returns allowed, remaining, reset_at; a policy object (key pattern, rate, burst, window, scope); response headers (RateLimit-*, Retry-After, status 429). Say that the limiter is a library plus a shared store, not a separate network hop, because of the latency budget.

0:10 to 0:20: High-level design and the diagram. Token bucket per key; local in-process buckets on each node for the fast path; a shared store (Redis-class) for the global count; policies loaded from a config service and cached. Explain the two-tier idea: local buckets take the decision, the shared store corrects them a few times per second.

0:20 to 0:40: Two deep dives. (1) Exactness versus cost: a fixed window per node allows up to N times the limit at window edges; a sliding window approximated from two fixed windows (the Cloudflare method) brings the average rate error to about 6 percent at the cost of two counters per key; an exact distributed token bucket needs an atomic read-modify-write on the shared store per request, which is the 1 ms you do not have at 50k per second across 20 nodes. Choose: local token buckets with a global budget split per node, re-split every 100 ms from the shared counts. (2) Failure modes: shared store down (fail open with local limits, alert; say why fail closed is wrong for a public API and right for a payment endpoint); hot key (one tenant at 40 percent of traffic: a dedicated shard or a local-only limit for that key); node restart (buckets start full; acceptable overshoot of one burst); clock skew (windows keyed on monotonic local time, store time only for TTL).

0:40 to 0:45: Evolution. Tiers and per-endpoint costs (cost parameter), limits per region, moving the policy store to the gateway, metrics: allowed, rejected, overshoot ratio per key, shared-store latency. Ask what the interviewer would like to see deeper. The level shows in the deep dives: L1 gives a correct single-store token bucket; L2 gives the two-tier design with the exactness trade-off and the fail-open argument; L3 asks whether the product needs a limiter at all or a cost-based quota, and reframes the hot tenant as a tenancy question.
Context and scope: The public API, its gateway fleet, the keys and tiers that exist today, and the incidents or abuse that motivate a limiter.
Goals and non-goals: Bound every key within 10 percent per second, add under 1 ms, never make the API unavailable; DDoS and billing out of scope.
Design: This answer fills it: local token buckets, the correction loop against the shared store, the policy service and the header contract.
Alternatives considered: Where the decision is made (shared store per request versus local with correction) and the algorithm choice, with the trade-off table.
Cross-cutting concerns: Observability of drift (allowed, rejected, overshoot ratio per key, store latency) and the fail-open policy as a security review item.
Review questions the doc must answer: The worst-case overshoot under a store outage, and the behaviour when the policy service is down.

sim.heading: Simulate the limiter
sim.caption: The model is one hot key behind one limiter, one API and one database. Read the scale note above the block before comparing its numbers with the exercise.
steps: Raise the offered load to 600 with the limit at 100 and the burst at 200: goodput holds at about 100 requests a second, p99 stays near 78 ms and the API is only about 41% busy.
That is the trade the limiter makes: predictable latency, bought by refusing most of the offered load, about 83% of requests here.

Now raise the limit to 600 and the burst to 400, which is no limit at all: p99 climbs to about 289 ms, the API saturates and about 60% of requests fail, shed by the API instead of refused by the limiter.
